# 60.4 Distinguish Eight Objects That Must Not Be Collapsed

The investigation fails at the first step if it treats different objects as one.

## 60.4.1 This chapter and Chapter 61’s full logic of Christ’s argument from the writing

Psalm 82 supplies the wording. Chapter 61 will show the logic by which He moves from that wording to the present charge, and the weight He assigns to the written text. This chapter must show why the wording as written is the material. Showing why the wording is used is not drawing the dedicated a fortiori. To treat this file as already Chapter 61 would steal the later logic. To refuse to ask why He uses the written wording would leave the assignment’s second sentence unperformed.

## 60.4.2 Exposition of Psalm 82 and the finished doctrine that the scripture cannot be broken

The psalm is Scripture. John 10:35 states that the scripture cannot be broken. Chapters 62–63 will examine that statement and its why. This chapter must treat the psalm as already standing writing. Treating it as standing writing is not the finished unbreakability-file. To consume Chapters 62–63 here would steal the later why. To omit the psalm’s standing as writing would make the citation a curiosity.

## 60.4.3 Psalm context and a blank check for later “gods” speculation

The psalm uses אֱלֹהִים of those it addresses. Later systems may wish to treat that vocabulary as a license for deification, for identity-teaching detached from judgment, or for a modern controversy as the center of the file. Context is the psalm’s judicial argument. A blank check is the refusal of that argument. This chapter is the second operation, not the first.

## 60.4.4 This chapter and Chapter 59’s Dedication-file

Chapter 59 located the citation in the blasphemy-dispute. This chapter locates the citation in the psalm. Neighbourhood is not identity. The Dedication scene remains premise. The psalm is the new object. Collapse of the two would hide the psalm inside a second scene-description.

## 60.4.5 The psalm’s judicial frame and a later scholarly quarrel as the chapter’s center

Verse 1 has been read, in later discussion, as a heavenly assembly or as a human court. The chapter will follow the psalm’s own verbs of judging, the mortality of verse 7, and Christ’s own characterization — those to whom the word of God came — rather than inventing a modern controversy as the center. Noting that later readers differ is not making their quarrel the object. The object is the text.

## 60.4.6 Naming of verse 6 and the whole psalm’s argument

Chapter 59 named verse 6. This chapter must give the relevant psalm, not the line alone. A named line without the indictment, the command, and the mortality-sentence is still a fragment. The assignment is the citation in context.

## 60.4.7 This chapter and the Chapter 65 gate

This chapter establishes that the cited wording stands as written Holy Writ already in force for His hearers, and that He argues from that wording. Chapter 65 will conclude that the Graphē is the primary written authority by which truth is known, tested, reasoned through, taught, discerned, and lived. Neighbourhood is not arrival.

## 60.4.8 Image or sonship correspondence and the psalm’s judicial address

Verse 6 also says, “all of you are children of the most High.” Genesis 1:26–27 records that God made man in His image. Correspondence of sonship-language is real and may be named. Correspondence is not a conversion of Psalm 82 into a later identity-lesson that ignores unjust judgment and death like men. The psalm remains a judicial address.

Thus:

> **The actual citation in Psalm 82’s context is this chapter’s object. It is not Chapter 61, not finished unbreakability, not a blank check for “gods” speculation, not Chapter 59 retried, not a modern quarrel as center, not a detached lemma, not the Graphē-gate, and not an identity-lesson that evacuates the judicial frame.**

---

# 60.5 Premises That May Be Used, and Premises That May Not

The chapter may use, as already in force:

- Truth as conformity to reality, distinct from belief, popularity, and institutional consensus (Chapters 1–3).
- Knowledge, evidence, reason, and rational warrant as inspectable operations (Chapters 4–7).
- God as the ground of truth, truthful, faithful, immutable, and incapable of falsehood (Chapters 10–12).
- γραφή (*graphē*, G1124) as writing that, in biblical usage, designates Holy Writ / Scripture (Chapters 20–22).
- Revelation given; inspiration of Scripture as writing; “all Scripture”; the sequence from communication to written testimony (Chapters 29–32).
- Authentication of the record as testimony (Chapters 33–42).
- Christ as historical, the Truth, authenticated in claims and works, crucified and raised, attested by positioned seers (Chapters 43–47).
- Christ’s confirmation of received Scripture as binding written word, including Law, Prophets, and Psalms (Chapter 48).
- The scriptural corpus, canon as recognition, prophetic and apostolic authority, unity of written testimony, distinction of operations, inspiration’s guarantees, infallibility of the record, and the synthesis of truth, authority, and the written Word (Chapters 51–58).
- John 10:34–36 as a complete argument in the Dedication controversy: appeal to what is written, citation named as Psalm 82:6, characterization of those to whom the word of God came, statement that the scripture cannot be broken belonging to the unit, application to the sanctified and sent Son (Chapter 59).

The chapter may not use, as if already finished:

- Christ’s reasoning from what is written as Movement VIII’s dedicated file (Chapter 61).
- The finished sense of “cannot be broken” and the dedicated “why” of that statement (Chapters 62–63).
- John 17:17 as finished Graphē-doctrine (Chapter 64).
- The Graphē as primary written authority in the Movement VIII sense (Chapter 65).
- Mishandling, tergiversation, ἄπειρος (*apeiros*, G552), σπουδάζω (*spoudazō*, G4704), and readiness for the Six First Principles.

The chapter may name those later questions as later. Naming is not consuming.

Thus:

> **Premises already earned may be used. Later verdicts may not be borrowed as if the citation-file had already become the dedicated reasoning, the finished why of unbreakability, or the Graphē-gate.**

---

# 60.6 The Sequence of Levels: One Clean Scope Section

What this chapter does not settle is a matter of sequence, not of doubt about what it does settle.

The investigation proceeds by levels. Each level answers its question with full force. The next level remains next because it is a different question.

**Already in force.** God cannot lie. Revelation has been given and authenticated. Scripture as writing is God-breathed. The record does not fail as truthful divine writing of what it actually communicates. The Graphē has authority as the written Word at the level earned through Movement VII. Christ is the historical Truth who confirms the Scriptures He received. John 10:34–36 is His appeal to what is written as decisive in the Dedication blasphemy-dispute. The cited wording has been named as Psalm 82:6.

**This level.** Given those premises, Psalm 82 is a judicial psalm whose verse 6 addresses as gods those who judge under God and to whom the word of God came. Christ uses that written wording because the case depends upon the words as written, already standing as Holy Writ for His hearers, not upon a paraphrase that would weaken the court. The warrant is full at this level. It is not postponed until Chapter 61 in order to keep the present conclusion weak.

**Next levels, named once.** Christ’s reasoning from what is written belongs to Chapter 61. “The scripture cannot be broken,” and why, belong to Chapters 62–63. John 17:17 belongs to Chapter 64. The Graphē as primary written authority belongs to Chapter 65. Skill, diligence, mishandling, and the First Principles remain later still.

**Limits that belong to this level itself, not to later hesitation.** The psalm’s context is not a fragment. Exposition of the psalm is not the dedicated a fortiori. Treating the wording as standing writing is not the finished why of unbreakability. The judicial frame is not a blank check for later “gods” speculation. Using Chapter 59 is not rewriting it. Those limits are part of what the citation-file is. They are not a stack of clauses designed to drain the positive conclusion.

The chapter will therefore state the positive warrant with full force, locate the limits as belonging to the doctrine rather than as apologies, and name later files once as later files. It will not repeat, under every paragraph, that the present conclusion is not proof of a later conclusion. Sequence is already the account of that difference.

Thus:

> **The present examination is in force at this level. Later verdicts remain later because they are different questions. Limits named here are the shape of the doctrine, not a delayed doubt about the doctrine.**

---

# 60.7 The Actual Citation Defined

**The actual citation**, in this chapter, is the written wording Christ quotes as already standing in their law, identified as Psalm 82:6, given in the words the writing uses rather than in a later summary of what the writing is “about.”

John 10:34:

> **“Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods?”**

Psalm 82:6:

> **“I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.”**

The citation is the first clause of the psalm-verse, in the form He quotes. The remainder of the verse belongs to the psalm’s context and will be examined with it. The citation is not less than the quoted words. It is not more than the quoted words plus the psalm that contains them.

Three false substitutes must be refused.

**A theme.** “The psalm is about judgment” may be true as a summary and still not be the citation. He does not ask whether a theme is in their law. He asks whether this wording is written.

**A later doctrinal expansion.** “Ye are gods” does not, by being cited, become a completed metaphysics of deification, a completed anthropology of image, or a completed Christology of the Son. Those expansions, if they come, must come by later argument. They do not come by the mere fact of quotation.

**A reconstructed original setting offered as the citation.** A later reconstruction of a court-scene, a festival, or a heavenly council may be offered as history. It is not the wording. The wording is what is written. Unverifiable reconstruction is refused as a substitute for the text.

The Greek of John 10:34, ἐγὼ εἶπα θεοί ἐστε, corresponds to the wording of the Greek Psalter at this verse. The correspondence is named as correspondence of written wording, not as an invented account of which physical copy He held. The argument depends upon what is written, not upon a reconstructed book-object in the porch.

Thus:

> **The actual citation is the written wording “I said, Ye are gods,” as Psalm 82:6 already stands. A theme, a later expansion, and an invented setting are not the citation.**

---

# 60.8 Psalm 82 Context Defined

**Psalm 82 context**, in this chapter, is the argument of the psalm as a whole: speaker, addressees, charge, command, address of verse 6, mortality-sentence, and closing appeal — the frame in which verse 6 is an address and not a proverb torn out of a book.

A psalm-context is not a caption. It is the sequence of sentences that makes verse 6 do the work it does. Remove verses 1–5, and “Ye are gods” has no judicial charge behind it. Remove verse 7, and the address has no mortality to qualify it. Remove verse 8, and the psalm has no appeal from failed human judgment to God’s judgment of the earth. The relevant text is therefore the psalm, not the fragment.

Context so defined is not a historical novel of Asaph’s career. The superscription names “A Psalm of Asaph.” The name locates the writing among the psalms so ascribed. It does not license a biography beyond the record. The investigation follows the sentences.

Two false substitutes must be refused.

**Immediate verbal neighbourhood without the argument.** One may quote verse 6 and call verses 5 and 7 “context” while still treating verse 6 as a slogan. Neighbourhood of words is not yet argumentative context. Argumentative context is the psalm’s case: God judging those who judge.

**A later controversy offered as context.** Later readers have disputed whether the “gods” of verse 1 are heavenly beings or human judges. That dispute may be noted as a later reading. It is not the psalm’s context. The psalm’s context is the psalm’s own verbs, addressees, and outcome. Christ’s characterization in John 10:35 is then the governing identification of those addressees for the citation’s use: those to whom the word of God came.

Thus:

> **Psalm 82 context is the psalm’s judicial argument as a whole. It is not a slogan’s caption, not invented colour, and not a later quarrel substituted for the text.**

---

# 60.9 Why Written Wording Defined

**Why Christ uses the written wording**, in this chapter, is the inspectable reason the case requires the words as they stand written, rather than a paraphrase, a theme, or a later restatement that would weaken or relocate the argument.

The definition has four elements.

First, **as written**. γεγραμμένον has already been established in Chapter 59 as the category of the appeal. The present file asks what follows for this sentence: the force is the words, not a speaker’s later equivalent.

Second, **rather than a paraphrase**. A paraphrase might say, “Scripture honours judges,” or “men have a high office,” or “God once spoke to Israel.” Each of those sentences might be related to the psalm. None of them is the wording the charge requires. The charge is that He, being a man, makes Himself God. The writing already contains “Ye are gods” as an address to those who received God’s word. Remove the word “gods,” and the writing no longer supplies the vocabulary the dispute has named.

Third, **as the material of a court already opened**. Chapter 59 opened the court. This chapter shows that the exhibit in that court is the wording. An exhibit that has been replaced by a summary is not the exhibit.

Fourth, **not the dedicated a fortiori**. Why this wording is used is not yet how the inference from this wording to “I am the Son of God” is drawn in full. The first is this file. The second is Chapter 61. The two are neighbours. They are not the same assignment.

Thus:

> **Why He uses the written wording is why the case requires the words as written rather than a paraphrase that would weaken the court. It is not yet Chapter 61’s dedicated logic.**

---

# 60.10 Lexical Control: אֱלֹהִים, εἶπα, θεοί

The psalm’s and the citation’s God-terms must be controlled, not inflated.

**אֱלֹהִים** (*elohim*, H430) is a plural form whose biblical usage includes the true God, false gods, and, in specified judicial contexts, those who sit in judgment. Lexical range is not contextual meaning. The word does not, by itself, prove deification, polytheism, or a later metaphysical system. Context must decide which use is in force in Psalm 82. The psalm itself uses the word of God who stands to judge (verse 1a) and of those among whom He judges (verse 1b; verse 6). The same form therefore appears in more than one role inside one psalm. That fact is not a license to collapse the Most High into the addressees, or the addressees into the Most High.

**אָמַרְתִּי** is the first-person perfect of אָמַר (*amar*, H559): I have said. Verse 6 presents the address as already spoken. The English of John 10:34, “I said,” and of Psalm 82:6, “I have said,” names the same completed speech. The citation is a citation of a saying already in force as said.

**θεοί** is the plural of θεός (*theos*, G2316): gods. John 10:34 quotes θεοί ἐστε — “ye are gods.” The Greek corresponds to the psalm’s אֱלֹהִים as rendered in the Greek Psalter. The term in the citation is the psalm’s term in Greek dress. It is not a new vocabulary invented for the porch.

Three refusals follow.

The terms do not, by themselves, finish Chapter 61. A named address may be located. How the Son’s argument uses that address remains later.

The terms do not, by themselves, finish “cannot be broken.” A named writing may be cited. Why it cannot be broken remains later.

The terms do not license a claim that every biblical use of אֱלֹהִים means the same thing. Context controls. Here the context is a psalm in which God judges those He has called gods, who judge unjustly, and who shall die like men.

Thus:

> **אֱלֹהִים and θεοί name, in this psalm and this citation, an address whose sense is controlled by the psalm’s judicial argument and by Christ’s characterization, not by an isolated lexicon-entry.**

---

# 60.11 Lexical Control of Neighbouring Terms Named, Not Exhausted

Other terms in the psalm must be named accurately and left, where the TOC requires, to later files or to their proper force here.

**אֵל** (*El*, H410) appears in verse 1 in the phrase commonly rendered “congregation of the mighty”: עֲדַת־אֵל, the congregation of God / El. The phrase locates the assembly as God’s assembly. It does not, by itself, settle a later quarrel about whether the assembly is heavenly or earthly. The verbs that follow will.

**עֶלְיוֹן** (*Elyon*, H5945), Most High, appears in verse 6: “children of the most High.” The title distinguishes the addressees from the One whose children they are called. Children of the Most High are not the Most High. The distinction belongs to the verse and will govern later refusals of blank-check speculation.

**שָׁפַט** (*shaphat*, H8199), to judge, is the psalm’s governing verb: He judgeth (verse 1); how long will ye judge unjustly (verse 2); do justice (verse 3); arise, O God, judge the earth (verse 8). Judicial action is not ornament. It is the psalm’s work.

**מוּת** (*muth*, H4191) underlies verse 7: “ye shall die like men.” Mortality is the psalm’s own qualification of the address in verse 6. Those called gods shall die like men. The verb forbids treating verse 6 as an ontological promotion that has no death on the other side of it.

**λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ** in John 10:35: “the word of God” came to those who were called gods. Chapter 59 named the phrase as part of the unit and reserved its mapping onto the psalm. This chapter performs that mapping so far as the psalm’s “I have said” and the addressees’ judicial commission require. It does not convert the phrase into a second inspiration-file.

**λυθῆναι** remains reserved. The unit contains “cannot be broken.” This chapter records that the writing now examined is the writing of which that clause is said. It does not define “broken.” It does not answer why.

Thus:

> **Neighbouring terms are named so the psalm is not mistranslated. Judge, Most High, die like men, and the word of God locate the frame. “Broken” remains quoted as belonging to the unit and reserved as a dedicated object.**

---

# 60.12 The Psalm Given in Full

The relevant text must be given as a complete argument, not as a proof-text fragment.

> **A Psalm of Asaph.**
>
> **God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods.**
>
> **How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah.**
>
> **Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy.**
>
> **Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked.**
>
> **They know not, neither will they understand; they walk on in darkness: all the foundations of the earth are out of course.**
>
> **I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.**
>
> **But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.**
>
> **Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations.**
> — Psalm 82:1–8

The eight verses are one psalm. The first sentence locates God as judge among those called gods. The next sentences charge, command, and diagnose. Verse 6 is the address already spoken. Verse 7 qualifies that address with mortality. Verse 8 appeals from the failed court to God’s judgment of the earth.

The argumentative force of the whole, at this stage, can be stated without stealing later files.

God stands. He does not leave judgment unattended.

He judges among gods. The addressees are already in a judicial frame before verse 6 is spoken.

He charges unjust judgment. The “gods” are not being flattered. They are being indicted.

He commands defense of the poor. Office is measured by justice to the weak, not by a title.

He diagnoses ignorance and darkness. The foundations are out of course. The crisis is judicial and moral, not a seminar about vocabulary.

He recalls what He has said: Ye are gods; children of the Most High. The address is prior speech, now cited inside the indictment.

He declares they shall die like men. The title does not confer immunity.

He appeals to God to judge the earth. Failed human judgment is not the last judgment.

That is the psalm in full argumentative force. A later preacher may quote only “Ye are gods.” A later controversy may quote only a theory of gods. Neither quotation is the argument. The argument is the psalm as given.

Thus:

> **The relevant text is Psalm 82 as a whole: God judging those called gods, charging unjust judgment, addressing them as gods and children of the Most High, declaring their death like men, and appealing to God to judge the earth. Fragmentation is not exposition.**

---

# 60.13 Superscription and Speaker: A Psalm of Asaph

The writing is superscribed “A Psalm of Asaph.”

The superscription locates the psalm among the Asaph psalms. It does not, in this chapter, become a biography of Asaph, a reconstructed liturgy, or an unverifiable account of first performance. The investigation takes the psalm as a writing already standing in the received Psalter, which Chapter 48 has already shown Christ to receive among the Scriptures, and which Chapter 59 has already shown Him to cite as written in their law.

The speaker of verse 1 is the psalm’s narrator presenting God as standing and judging. The speaker of verses 2–4 is God addressing the addressees. Verse 5 diagnoses their condition. Verse 6 is God’s prior address recalled: “I have said.” Verse 7 continues the divine sentence. Verse 8 is the psalm’s appeal to God.

“I have said” in verse 6 is therefore not a later commentator’s gloss. It is the psalm’s own presentation of a saying of God already in force. When Christ quotes “I said, Ye are gods,” He quotes that saying as written. He does not invent a speaker. He does not transfer the saying to a private voice of His own as if the psalm had never spoken.

The Bible Introduction’s larger argument that the received writings were already treated as Scripture in Christ’s scene is used here only as already-established correspondence: a psalm is cited as law. Correspondence is not a second confirmation-trial, and not a second canon-file.

Thus:

> **The psalm stands as an Asaph psalm in the received Psalter. “I have said” is God’s prior address as the psalm presents it. Location of the writing is not a reconstructed career of Asaph.**

---

# 60.14 Verse 1: God Standing in the Congregation, Judging Among the Gods

Verse 1 opens the frame.

> **“God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods.”**

Two acts are named.

**He stands.** God takes His place in the assembly. The congregation is not unsupervised. Judgment is not left to those who happen to sit.

**He judges among the gods.** The addressees of the psalm are already called gods before verse 6 recalls the saying. The title, whatever its force, is already in the frame as the designation of those among whom God judges.

The verse therefore forbids two opposite errors.

**Error of flattening.** Flattening says that “gods” in verse 1a and “gods” in verse 1b must mean the same referent in the same role, so that God is judging Himself, or so that there is no Most High distinct from the assembly. The verse distinguishes the One who stands and judges from those among whom He judges.

**Error of detaching verse 6.** Detaching says that “Ye are gods” is a sudden metaphysical announcement. Verse 1 has already placed “gods” in a judicial assembly. Verse 6 will recall what has been said of those who sit there.

Later readers have asked whether the assembly is heavenly or earthly. The question may be named. It is not this chapter’s center. The verse’s own contribution is already full: God judges in an assembly of those called gods. Verses 2–7 will show what those addressees do, what they fail to do, and how they die. Christ’s own characterization will then identify them, for the citation’s use, as those to whom the word of God came.

Thus:

> **Verse 1 locates God as judge in an assembly of those called gods. The frame is judicial before verse 6 is recalled. A later quarrel about the assembly’s metaphysics is not the verse’s assignment.**

---

# 60.15 Verses 2–4: The Judicial Charge

Verses 2–4 are the indictment and the command.

> **“How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah.”**
> — Psalm 82:2

> **“Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy. Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked.”**
> — Psalm 82:3–4

The second-person verbs are judicial verbs. “How long will ye judge unjustly” names their office as judging and their failure as injustice. “Accept the persons of the wicked” names partiality. The commands that follow — defend, do justice, deliver, rid — are the measures of that office. The poor, the fatherless, the afflicted, and the needy are the persons by whom the court is tested.

These verses establish, with full force, that the addressees function as judges. Whatever else a later system may wish to say about “gods,” the psalm’s own sentences address them as those who judge, who can judge unjustly, and who are commanded to do justice to the weak. A reading that cannot account for unjust judgment, partiality, and the defense of the fatherless has not yet read the psalm.

The charge also establishes that the title in verse 6 is not a compliment that ends the case. The saying “Ye are gods” will be recalled inside an indictment, not as an escape from it. Office under God is compatible with failure before God. The psalm is about that compatibility, and about its consequence in verse 7.

Thus:

> **Verses 2–4 address the “gods” as judges: they judge unjustly, they are commanded to defend the poor. The judicial frame is the psalm’s own, not a later imposition.**

---

# 60.16 Verse 5: Ignorance, Darkness, Foundations Out of Course

Verse 5 diagnoses the condition of those so addressed.

> **“They know not, neither will they understand; they walk on in darkness: all the foundations of the earth are out of course.”**

Not knowing and not understanding are not compliments. Walking in darkness is not a mystical ascent. The foundations of the earth out of course is the psalm’s own measure of how serious unjust judgment is. The crisis is not a private mood. It is a disorder of the foundations.

The verse matters for the citation because it forbids treating “Ye are gods” as a statement of present competence. Those called gods, in this psalm, do not know, do not understand, and walk in darkness. The address in verse 6 is therefore not the psalm’s last word about them. It is a prior saying now set beside their failure.

Christ’s later characterization — those to whom the word of God came — is compatible with this diagnosis. The word may come, and the hearers may still not know. Receiving the word as office is not the same act as walking in the light of it. The psalm records both the coming of the address and the darkness of those addressed. Chapter 61 will use that structure so far as the dedicated reasoning requires. This chapter needs only the diagnosis: verse 6 is not a certificate of present enlightenment.

Thus:

> **Verse 5 diagnoses those called gods as not knowing, not understanding, walking in darkness. The address of verse 6 is recalled inside failure, not as a slogan of present competence.**

---

# 60.17 Verse 6: The Address — “I Have Said, Ye Are Gods”

Verse 6 is the cited wording in its place.

> **“I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.”**

Four features of the sentence must be seen.

**It is prior speech.** “I have said” presents the address as already spoken. The psalm does not now invent the title. It recalls it. Christ’s “I said” is that recall quoted as written.

**It is second-person address.** “Ye are gods” is spoken to the addressees of verses 2–4. It is not a general proverb about the universe. It is not an abstract definition of deity. It is “ye.”

**It is the vocabulary of gods.** The word is the word. The investigation does not replace it with a weaker English substitute in order to spare later embarrassment, and it does not inflate it into a later system in order to satisfy later appetite. The writing says gods. The writing must be allowed to say it.

**It is paired with sonship-language.** “Children of the most High” stands in the same verse. The addressees are called gods and called children of Elyon. The pairing will be examined in the next section. It already shows that the verse itself supplies a relation to the Most High rather than an identity with the Most High.

At this stage, the verse’s contribution to the citation is already full. This is the wording. This is its place: after indictment, before mortality. This is its form: prior divine speech to those who judge. Chapter 59 named the verse. This section locates it inside the psalm. Location inside the psalm is the difference between a lemma and a citation in context.

Thus:

> **Verse 6 is God’s prior address to the psalm’s addressees: Ye are gods; children of the Most High. The citation is this wording in this place, not a detached shock-phrase.**

---

# 60.18 “And All of You Are Children of the Most High”

The second clause of verse 6 must not be dropped, and it must not be allowed to steal the file.

> **“…and all of you are children of the most High.”**

**What the clause is.** It is a parallel address. Those called gods are also called children of Elyon. “All of you” distributes the address across the assembly, not to one isolated figure.

**What the clause does.** It relates the addressees to the Most High as children to Father, not as rivals who have become the Most High. Sonship-language in Scripture can name Israel, can name kings, can name those who belong to God. The present verse uses it of the same persons who judge unjustly and who shall die like men. The clause therefore belongs to office and relation under God, not to an escape from God.

**What the clause does not do here.** It does not finish a doctrine of adoption. It does not finish a doctrine of the image of God. It does not finish the Son’s unique relation to the Father, already examined as identity and claim in Chapters 44–45 and applied in John 10:36. It does not become a later identity-lesson that every hearer is already “gods” in a sense that would make the blasphemy-charge unintelligible.

Genesis 1:26–27 records that God made man in His image, after His likeness. That record stands. A later leaflet-argument that places Psalm 82:6 beside Genesis 1:26 as language of man’s true nature may be reconstructed as a proposed correspondence: children of the Most High and image-language both speak of relation to God. Correspondence is not identity of assignment. Genesis 1 is the making of man. Psalm 82 is the judging of those who judge. The image does not evacuate the indictment. The indictment does not deny that man was made in the image. The two writings remain two. This chapter’s object is the psalm’s address in its judicial frame.

Thus:

> **“Children of the most High” relates the addressees to God without identifying them as the Most High. Image-language may be named as correspondence. It may not convert Psalm 82 into a blank check.**

---

# 60.19 Verse 7: Mortality and Fall — They Shall Die Like Men

Verse 7 is the psalm’s own qualification of verse 6.

> **“But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.”**

The adversative is the psalm’s. “I have said, Ye are gods” is not left without a “but.” Those so addressed shall die like men. They shall fall like a prince. The title does not confer deathlessness. The office does not confer immunity.

This verse is decisive for the addressees. Whatever later quarrel may be raised about verse 1, verse 7 names their end in the language of human death and princely fall. The psalm itself therefore places the “gods” of verse 6 on the side of those who die as men die. A reading that cannot hear “die like men” as the psalm’s own check upon “Ye are gods” has not yet read the psalm.

The verse also matters for Christ’s use. He cites verse 6, not verse 7. He does not thereby cancel verse 7. He cites the address as written. The address, in the psalm, is the address of those who remain mortal. The persons to whom the word of God came were called gods, and they remain those who die. That fact belongs to the written case. It will belong to Chapter 61 so far as the dedicated reasoning compares their calling with the Father’s sanctifying and sending of the Son. This chapter needs the qualification as the psalm’s own: the wording “Ye are gods” is not, in Psalm 82, a sentence of immortal deity.

Thus:

> **Verse 7 qualifies verse 6: those called gods shall die like men. The citation of the address does not cancel the psalm’s mortality-sentence, and the mortality-sentence forbids treating the address as a grant of deathless deity.**

---

# 60.20 Verse 8: Appeal to God to Judge the Earth

Verse 8 closes the psalm.

> **“Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations.”**

Failed judgment in the assembly is not the last judgment. The psalm appeals to God to arise and judge the earth. The inheritance of the nations is assigned to Him. The Most High remains the judge of the whole, not merely the supervisor of a local court.

The closing matters for context because it shows what the psalm is for. It is not a hymn to the addressees. It is a cry from their failure to God’s judgment. “Ye are gods” is not the psalm’s destination. God’s judging the earth is the psalm’s destination.

Christ’s citation of verse 6 therefore takes a line from a psalm that ends by appealing past those who were called gods. He does not cite a psalm whose point is to make men into the Most High. He cites a psalm whose point is that God judges those who judge, and that God must yet judge the earth. The later application in John 10:36 to the One the Father sanctified and sent will have this psalm, not a rival psalm, as its written material. The dedicated application remains Chapter 61. The psalm’s destination is already this file’s to state.

Thus:

> **Verse 8 appeals from the failed court to God’s judgment of the earth. The psalm’s destination is God’s judging, not the addressees’ deification. That destination is part of the citation’s context.**

---

# 60.21 The Psalm’s Argument as a Whole

The verses now stand together as one argument.

God takes His place in the assembly and judges among those called gods (v. 1). He charges them with unjust judgment and partiality (v. 2). He commands justice for the poor, the fatherless, the afflicted, and the needy (vv. 3–4). He diagnoses their ignorance, darkness, and the disorder of the foundations (v. 5). He recalls His prior address: Ye are gods; children of the Most High (v. 6). He declares their death like men and their fall like princes (v. 7). He appeals to God to judge the earth and inherit the nations (v. 8).

The argument is therefore this:

> **Those who judge under God have been addressed as gods and as children of the Most High; they have judged unjustly; they remain mortal; God Himself must judge.**

That is the psalm’s case. Verse 6 is a member of the case. It is the prior address. It is not the whole case. A reading that treats verse 6 as the whole psalm has not read the psalm. A reading that treats the judicial verbs as optional colour around a metaphysical slogan has not read the psalm.

The argument as a whole is what Chapter 59 reserved when it named the psalm and refused to exposit it. The reservation is now performed. The psalm is a judicial psalm. The cited wording is the address inside that judicial psalm.

Thus:

> **Psalm 82’s argument is God’s judgment of those He has addressed as gods, who judge unjustly and shall die like men, with appeal to God to judge the earth. Verse 6 belongs to that argument and does not replace it.**

---

# 60.22 To Whom the Address Is Directed

The question of addressees must now be answered from the psalm’s own frame, not from a later appetite.

**In the psalm’s own sentences.** The addressees are those among whom God judges (v. 1); those who judge unjustly and accept the wicked (v. 2); those commanded to defend the poor and fatherless (vv. 3–4); those who do not know and walk in darkness (v. 5); those told they shall die like men and fall like princes (v. 7). The only description that fits all of those sentences without remainder is: those who exercise judgment under God and are accountable to Him for it.

**Judges**, in this argument, names that function. It does not require a reconstructed organigram of a particular court. It does not require an invented roster of names. It names what the verbs name: they judge. The poor and fatherless are the persons of their office. Death like men is their end. Princes are the comparison of their fall.

**Not the Most High.** Verse 6 calls them children of the Most High. Verse 8 calls God to arise and judge the earth. The addressees are not the One who inherits the nations.

**Not a blank “everyone.”** “All of you” in verse 6 is all of the assembly addressed, not all later readers of the psalm in every sense a later teacher may wish. The address has a “ye.” The “ye” is the court that has failed.

The chapter does not invent a modern controversy as the center of this identification. Later readers who prefer a heavenly council as verse 1’s assembly must still account for unjust judging of the poor, for dying like men, and for Christ’s own words. The psalm’s verbs and the citation’s characterization govern. A later preference does not.

Thus:

> **The address “Ye are gods” is directed, in the psalm’s own frame, to those who judge under God — the assembly God judges, who fail the poor, who shall die like men — not to the Most High, and not to an unbounded later “everyone.”**

---

# 60.23 Christ’s Identification: Those to Whom the Word of God Came

John 10:35 supplies the governing identification of the cited persons for the argument in which the citation is used.

> **“If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came…”**

Chapter 59 established that this clause treats the citation as a written case: persons to whom the word of God came were called gods. This chapter maps that characterization onto the psalm.

**The mapping is inspectable.** Psalm 82:6 is God’s saying: “I have said.” A saying of God is the word of God coming to those addressed. The addressees of verses 2–4 are the “ye” of that saying. Christ names them as those to whom the word of God came. He does not name a different cast. He names the psalm’s addressees by the psalm’s own act: the word came; they were called gods.

**The mapping is not a second psalm.** He does not replace Psalm 82 with a new narrative. He reads the psalm as a case of the word of God coming. “Came” is the arrival of that word to them. The perfect of “I have said” is that arrival as already accomplished speech.

**The mapping governs later speculation.** If a later system wishes to make the “gods” of verse 6 a class to whom no word of God came, it has already left Christ’s identification. If a later system wishes to make them a class for whom “gods” means the Most High Himself, it has already left both the psalm’s “children of the most High” and Christ’s distinction between those called gods and the One the Father sanctified and sent.

The identification is therefore the psalm and the citation together, not the psalm against the citation, and not the citation against the psalm. Those to whom the word of God came are the judges of the psalm’s frame, addressed as gods by God’s prior speech.

Thus:

> **Christ identifies the cited persons as those to whom the word of God came. That identification maps onto Psalm 82’s “I have said” addressed to those who judge. The mapping is the citation’s own reading of the psalm, not a rival psalm.**

---

# 60.24 Judges in the Biblical Record: Elohim in Judicial Function

The psalm does not stand as a unique linguistic accident. Other writings already use אֱלֹהִים in judicial settings. Those writings are correspondence, not a second object, and not a reconstructed history of a particular court.

Exodus 21:6 and 22:8–9 bring parties “unto the judges,” where the Hebrew uses אֱלֹהִים. Exodus 22:28 joins “the gods” and “the ruler of thy people” in a prohibition of reviling. Deuteronomy 1:16–17 charges judges to hear causes and not to respect persons, “for the judgment is God’s.” 2 Chronicles 19:6–7 charges judges to take heed, “for ye judge not for man, but for the LORD, who is with you in the judgment.”

The correspondence is this: in the received writings, those who sit in judgment may be named with the God-word because judgment is God’s, and they judge under Him. The name is office under God, not identity as the Most High. The charge in Deuteronomy and Chronicles is the same species of charge as Psalm 82:2–4: judge righteously; do not respect persons.

This correspondence does not prove, by itself, every later theory of the psalm. It does establish that reading Psalm 82’s addressees as judges is not an imposition from outside the corpus. It is a reading the corpus already makes available by its own usage. Christ’s “word of God came” then names the commission: the word that constitutes them in that office has come.

The correspondence is used at proportional force. It is not a catalogue of every court in Israel. It is not an invented reconstruction of the Sanhedrin as if John 10 required that organigram. It is biblical usage illuminating biblical usage.

Thus:

> **Biblical usage already names judges with אֱלֹהִים because judgment is God’s. Psalm 82’s judicial addressees stand inside that usage. Correspondence is not a reconstructed court-history, and it is not the Most High flattened into the bench.**

---

# 60.25 The Word of God Coming: Commission, Not Deification

“The word of God came” must be given a precise sense, neither too thin nor too thick.

Too thin: the phrase means only that a copy of a psalm existed. Existence of a writing is already γεγραμμένον. “Came” names arrival to persons. The word reached them as address.

Too thick: the phrase means that those persons became the Most High, or became ontologically what the Son is. The psalm forbids this by “children of the most High” and by “die like men.” John 10 forbids this by distinguishing those so called from the One the Father sanctified and sent.

The warranted sense at this level is **commissioning address**. God has spoken to them. He has called them gods. He has called them children of the Most High. That speech locates them in office under Him: they judge; they are accountable; they remain men who die. The word coming is the arrival of that address, not a transformation into deathless deity.

The Aletheia leaflet’s placement of Psalm 82:6 beside Genesis 1:26 as language of man’s true nature may be reconstructed without being adopted as this chapter’s center. The reconstruction is: if man is made in God’s image, sonship-language is not foreign to the corpus. The limit is: Psalm 82 is not Genesis 1, and John 10 is not a later identity-lesson. Commission is not deification. Image is not a grant to evacuate the indictment. The word coming is the psalm’s “I have said,” not a later slogan that the hearer is already what the Most High is.

Thus:

> **“The word of God came” names commissioning address to those who judge under God. It is not the mere existence of a book, and it is not deification. Commission remains commission.**

---

# 60.26 Correspondence of Psalm 82:6 to John 10:34

The citation and the psalm now stand in inspectable correspondence.

| Member | Psalm 82 | John 10:34–35 |
|---|---|---|
| Prior speech | “I have said” | “I said” |
| Address | “Ye are gods” | “Ye are gods” |
| Relation | “children of the most High” | those to whom the word of God came |
| Frame | God judging those who judge | written in your law |
| Qualification in the psalm | shall die like men | (cited as the written case, not cancelled) |

The correspondence is verbal where the citation is verbal: “I said, Ye are gods” is Psalm 82:6’s first clause as written. The correspondence is interpretive where Christ names the addressees: “unto whom the word of God came” is His characterization of the psalm’s “ye,” not a different cast of characters.

What the table does not do is equally important. It does not draw the dedicated a fortiori of verse 36. It does not define “broken.” It does not claim that every later use of “gods” is this use. It shows that the citation is the psalm, and that the characterization is the psalm’s addressees under the psalm’s own act of divine speech.

The Greek correspondence of ἐγὼ εἶπα θεοί ἐστε to the Greek Psalter’s wording at this verse is named as written correspondence. It confirms that the argument is an argument from wording, not from a vague recollection of a theme. It does not become a reconstructed history of a particular scroll in Solomon’s porch.

Thus:

> **John 10:34–35 corresponds to Psalm 82:6 as written wording plus characterization of the addressees as those to whom the word of God came. Correspondence of citation is not yet the dedicated reasoning of verse 36.**

---

# 60.27 Why the Written Wording Matters: Citation, Not Paraphrase

The assignment’s second sentence can now be performed with full force.

Christ uses the written wording because the case is a case about words already standing, not a case about a speaker’s later equivalent.

The blasphemy-charge has named God. “Thou, being a man, makest thyself God.” The dispute’s vocabulary is already the God-vocabulary. He does not change the subject. He asks whether it is written, “I said, Ye are gods.” The writing already uses that vocabulary of those to whom the word of God came. The court therefore already contains the word the charge has used.

If He had paraphrased, He would have left the court without the exhibit. A paraphrase might be true as far as it went and still not be what is written. The appeal’s first move is γεγραμμένον. What is written is the wording. The wording is “Ye are gods.” That is why the wording matters: not because the chapter is about gods as a topic, but because the writing’s words are the material of a writing-argument.

Chapter 48 already established that He treats wording as having force, and that “it is written again” may judge a use of Scripture by Scripture. This scene is that practice under a capital charge. The present file’s contribution is not a second confirmation-trial. It is the reason this psalm’s words, as words, are the words He uses: they are the standing address the charge has made relevant, and they are written.

Thus:

> **He cites what is written, not a paraphrase, because a writing-argument requires the words as the exhibit. The God-vocabulary of the charge is already in the psalm as address to those who received God’s word.**

---

# 60.28 What a Paraphrase Would Weaken

The reason can be shown by contrast. The contrast is not a historical claim that He considered and rejected drafts. It is a rational account of why the wording as written is the wording the case needs.

**A paraphrase that avoided “gods.”** “Scripture honours those who judge.” The sentence might be related to the psalm. It would not place the word “gods” in the court. The charge is about making Himself God. A court without the word is a weaker court for that charge.

**A paraphrase that inflated “gods.”** “Scripture teaches that men are the Most High.” The psalm does not teach that. Verse 6’s sonship-clause, verse 7’s death, and verse 8’s appeal to God all forbid it. An inflated paraphrase would not be the writing. It would be a new claim wearing the writing’s clothes.

**A paraphrase that turned the psalm into a theme of judgment only.** “God judges unjust judges.” True as a summary of verses 1–5 and 8. It would omit the address that verse 6 actually speaks. The citation is the address. A theme of judgment without the address is not the citation.

**A paraphrase that made the scene about deification as a topic.** “Let us discuss whether men may be called gods.” That discussion would be a later seminar. It would not be “Is it not written.” The form would have changed from citation to symposium.

Each paraphrase weakens or relocates the case. The written wording does not. That is why He uses it. The reason is already full at this level. The dedicated drawing of verse 36 remains later. The present conclusion does not wait for that later drawing in order to be a conclusion: the exhibit is the words.

Thus:

> **A paraphrase that avoided, inflated, thematized, or seminarized the wording would weaken or relocate the case. The written wording is the exhibit the court requires.**

---

# 60.29 “I Said” as Standing Speech Already Written

“I said” / “I have said” is not filler.

In the psalm, אָמַרְתִּי presents the address as already spoken. In John 10:34, εἶπα presents that same completed speech as what is written in their law. The saying is not being composed in the porch. It is being cited as already in force.

Two consequences follow.

**The wording is not Christ’s improvisation.** He does not, in this move, offer a new oracle. He offers their writing. The force of the words is the force of a saying already said and already written. Chapter 59 established that the appeal is not mere opinion. This section locates that conclusion in the grammar of the citation: “I have said” is prior speech.

**The wording is not a dead relic.** Prior speech, as written, remains available as a case. He does not say, “It was once said, and it no longer matters.” He says it is written. Standing speech is speech that still stands. Why it cannot be broken remains Chapters 62–63. That it is treated as standing is already this file’s to state, because otherwise “I have said” would be an archive label rather than a court exhibit.

The speaker of the psalm’s “I have said” is God in the psalm’s presentation. Christ quotes that “I said” as written law. He does not, in this chapter, become a second author of Psalm 82. He becomes the One who argues from Psalm 82 as written. The dedicated weight of that act belongs in part to Chapter 61. The fact of the act — citation of standing speech — belongs here.

Thus:

> **“I said” names standing speech already written: prior divine address, now cited as law, not improvisation and not a dead relic. Standing as written is this level’s conclusion, not yet the finished why of unbreakability.**

---

# 60.30 The Psalm as Already Holy Writ for His Hearers

The citation functions because the psalm already stands as Holy Writ for those He answers.

Chapter 59 established that “your law” names the received written Scripture they already acknowledge, and that the appeal binds them by a writing they cannot recuse as foreign. This chapter adds what that standing means for this psalm.

Psalm 82 is not a foreign hymn introduced as a curiosity. It is a psalm in the received Psalter. He cites it as γεγραμμένον in their law. They are not being asked to accept a new book. They are being asked to admit a wording in a book they already have.

The Bible Introduction’s observation that the received Old Testament writings were not, in that scene, an open controversy about identity of corpus, is reconstructible without a second canon-file. The appeal works because the writing’s identity as Scripture is common ground. Chapter 52 already examined recognition. Chapter 48 already examined confirmation of Law, Prophets, and Psalms. This chapter uses that common ground as the condition of this psalm’s force: the wording stands as written Holy Writ already in force for His hearers.

“Already in force” at this level means: the words are available as court-material without a prior debate, in this scene, about whether the psalm is Scripture. It does not mean that Chapter 65’s gate has been drawn. It does not mean that every later hearer in every later century has been examined. It means what the scene exhibits: He argues from this psalm as their law.

Thus:

> **Psalm 82 stands as written Holy Writ already in force for His hearers. The citation is an appeal to a psalm they already have, not an introduction of a foreign book. Standing as their law is not yet the Graphē-gate.**

---

# 60.31 Positive Warrant: Scripture-Governed Argument

The positive warrant can now be stated with full force, without a stack of postponements.

Christ is the Truth already identified. He confirms received Scripture already. The Graphē has standing as the written Word already. John 10:34–36 is already His appeal to what is written in a blasphemy-dispute. The writing He cites is Psalm 82, a judicial psalm in which God addresses as gods those who judge under Him, who have received His word, who fail the poor, and who shall die like men. He quotes the written wording of verse 6, not a paraphrase, because the case requires the words as the exhibit: the God-vocabulary of the charge is already in the writing as address to those to whom the word of God came. That act is Scripture-governed argument: the psalm’s wording stands as written Holy Writ already in force for His hearers, and He argues from that wording as wording.

The warrant is a conjunction.

**What is cited:** Psalm 82:6, “I have said, Ye are gods,” inside Psalm 82’s judicial argument.

**To whom the psalm speaks:** those who judge under God, children of the Most High, mortal, those to whom the word of God came.

**How it is cited:** as written in their law, in the words that stand, not as a theme and not as a later equivalent.

**Why the words as words:** the charge has named God; the writing already uses that vocabulary of commissioned hearers; a paraphrase would weaken the exhibit.

**What that act is:** Scripture-governed argument — the court opened in Chapter 59 now supplied with its exhibit.

Remove any member, and the citation-file does not remain intact. Remove the psalm’s argument, and verse 6 is a shock-phrase. Remove the addressees as judges / those to whom the word came, and “gods” becomes a later speculation. Remove the written wording, and the appeal is a summary. Remove the charge’s vocabulary, and the reason for this wording is hidden. The conjunction is the warrant.

The warrant does not wait for Chapter 61 in order to be a warrant. Chapter 61 will show the logic from this exhibit to the Son-claim. This chapter answers that the exhibit is this psalm’s wording in this psalm’s frame, used as written because the case requires the words. That answer is already full. It is not the later answer. Full at this level is not premature at the next level.

Thus:

> **The investigator is warranted, with full force, in receiving the citation of Psalm 82:6 as Scripture-governed argument: the psalm’s judicial address stands as written Holy Writ already in force, and He cites the wording rather than a paraphrase that would weaken the case.**

---

# 60.32 The Judicial Frame Is Not Optional Ornament

The judicial frame must be stated as necessary, or later speculation will treat it as optional colour around a preferred word.

Without verses 2–4, “Ye are gods” has no office. Without verse 7, it has no mortality. Without verse 8, it has no appeal past the addressees to God. Without verse 1, it has no assembly in which God judges. The frame is not a preface. It is the argument.

Christ’s own characterization confirms the necessity of the frame. He does not say, “If he called them gods,” and stop. He says, “unto whom the word of God came.” The word coming is the frame’s commissioning act. He argues from a written case, not from an isolated title.

A later reading that keeps “gods” and discards the poor, the fatherless, unjust judgment, and death like men has not kept the citation. It has kept a word. The citation is the word in the case. The case is judicial.

This necessity does not steal Chapter 61. It supplies Chapter 61 with the right exhibit. An exhibit stripped of its frame would force the later file to reason from a fragment. The present file’s refusal of ornament-status for the frame is therefore part of serving the later file, not of performing it.

Thus:

> **The judicial frame is the psalm’s argument, not optional colour. Discarding unjust judgment, the poor, and death like men is discarding the citation’s context.**

---

# 60.33 Image and Sonship Language Without Blank Check

A related correspondence must be located and limited in one place, so that it neither governs the chapter nor is denied as if the verse had no second clause.

Verse 6 says, “all of you are children of the most High.” Genesis 1:26–27 says God made man in His image, after His likeness. John 1:12 speaks of power to become the sons of God. These writings exist. A reconstructed leaflet-argument that sets Psalm 82:6 beside the image as language of man’s true nature is therefore not a citation of nothing. It is a proposed join of sonship-language.

The join is not this chapter’s object, and it is not this chapter’s conclusion.

**What may be said.** Sonship-language in verse 6 is real. It distinguishes the addressees from the Most High while relating them to Him. Image of God is a biblical making of man, not a later invention. The corpus can speak of men in relation to God without speaking only of the unique Son.

**What may not be said here.** That Psalm 82 is a completed anthropology. That “Ye are gods” is a grant of the Most High’s identity to every later hearer. That the blasphemy-charge is unintelligible because everyone is already gods. That Genesis 1 has been retried. That the First Principles have been opened. That John 17:17 has been examined.

The blank check is the move from a real clause to an unbounded later use. This chapter refuses the move without refusing the clause. The clause remains: children of the Most High, who judge unjustly, who shall die like men, to whom the word of God came. That is already a full reading of the clause in this psalm. It is not a later curriculum of identity.

Thus:

> **Sonship-language in verse 6 is real and bounded by the judicial frame. Image-correspondence may be named. Neither is a blank check for later “gods” speculation, and neither is this chapter’s center.**

---

# 60.34 What the Citation Explicitly Establishes at This Stage

The record is explicit on the following, and this chapter claims them as explicit.

- Psalm 82 is a complete psalm in which God stands in the congregation and judges among those called gods (Psalm 82:1).
- Those addressees are charged with judging unjustly and accepting the wicked (Psalm 82:2).
- They are commanded to defend the poor and fatherless and to deliver the needy (Psalm 82:3–4).
- They are diagnosed as not knowing, not understanding, walking in darkness, with the foundations out of course (Psalm 82:5).
- God has said, “Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High” (Psalm 82:6).
- They shall die like men and fall like princes (Psalm 82:7).
- The psalm appeals to God to arise and judge the earth (Psalm 82:8).
- Christ cites the wording “I said, Ye are gods” as written in their law (John 10:34).
- He identifies those so called as those to whom the word of God came (John 10:35).
- The cited wording is the wording of Psalm 82:6.

Those are not inferences from a later system of deification. They are the psalm, the citation, and the characterization.

Thus:

> **What is explicit is the psalm’s judicial argument, the address of verse 6, the mortality of verse 7, the citation of that wording, and Christ’s identification of the addressees as those to whom the word of God came.**

---

# 60.35 What This Chapter Does Not Yet Establish

The same honesty requires a list of what this chapter does not claim to have finished, not as doubt about the citation, but as the shape of the movement.

- It has not followed His reasoning from the written wording as the dedicated object, nor stated in full the weight He assigns to that wording in the move to the Son-claim (Chapter 61).
- It has not defined “broken,” nor answered why the scripture cannot be broken from what Scripture is (Chapters 62–63).
- It has not examined John 17:17, “thy word is truth,” as Graphē-doctrine (Chapter 64).
- It has not concluded that the Graphē is the primary written authority by which truth is known, tested, reasoned through, taught, discerned, and lived (Chapter 65).
- It has not written Movement IX’s mishandling-files, nor Movement X’s labour-files, nor the Six First Principles.

The list is sequence. Sequence is not a second conclusion that the citation-file is weak.

Thus:

> **The citation’s context does not consume the later files. The later files do not postpone the citation’s context. Each question remains its own question.**

---

# 60.36 Competing Claim: “Gods” as the Whole Point Without the Judicial Frame

The first live reduction is topical capture by the word “gods” without the psalm’s judicial argument.

The reduction says: the interesting thing in Psalm 82:6 is a theory of gods; the judges, the poor, the fatherless, and death like men are incidentals; John 10 is a debate about deification in which the Graphē is a pretext.

The reduction fails for reasons already in the psalm and in the citation.

The psalm’s first verb of the addressees is judging. Its commands are justice to the weak. Its qualification is death like men. Its destination is God’s judging the earth. Verse 6 is the prior address inside that argument. An isolated “gods” is not Psalm 82.

Christ’s first move is not a theory of gods. It is “Is it not written.” His characterization is not a metaphysics. It is “unto whom the word of God came.” The Graphē is not a pretext. It is the court.

Chapter 59 already refused the reduction at the level of the passage. This chapter refuses it at the level of the psalm. The wording matters as writing inside a judicial case. Seriousness about the word “gods” is required because He cites it. Seriousness that discards the case is not seriousness about the citation. It is capture.

Thus:

> **Treating “gods” as the whole point without the judicial frame fails. The address belongs to those who judge under God, fail the poor, and die like men. A slogan is not the psalm.**

---

# 60.37 Competing Claim: Ignoring That Christ Appeals to Written Law

The second live reduction is to treat the scene as if the psalm were a convenient illustration, or as if the argument were a new oracle, or as if the words could be replaced by a later equivalent without loss.

The reduction says: what matters is His authority in the moment; the psalm is colour; wording is optional.

The reduction fails because the first word of the answer is a question about what is written. γεγραμμένον is not colour. “Your law” is not colour. “I said, Ye are gods” is not colour. A speaker who could have answered by mere assertion answers by citation. Chapter 59 established that this is not mere opinion. This chapter has shown that the exhibit is this psalm’s wording. Ignoring the appeal to written law is ignoring the argument’s first move.

The reduction also fails as architecture. The locked assignment is to examine the actual citation and to reason through why He uses the written wording. A reading that treats wording as optional has refused the assignment. The present file is the assignment, not the refusal of it.

Thus:

> **Ignoring that He appeals to written law fails. The citation is the argument’s exhibit. Wording is not optional colour around a new oracle.**

---

# 60.38 Competing Claim: This Chapter as Already Chapters 61–65

The third live reduction is architectural collapse.

The reduction says: once Psalm 82 has been read, the logic to the Son is finished, unbreakability is finished, “thy word is truth” is finished, and the Graphē-gate is finished.

The reduction fails because those are different questions.

Chapter 61 asks how the inference from this wording to the present charge holds, and what weight the written text is assigned in that inference. This chapter has shown why the wording as written is the material. Material is not the dedicated inference.

Chapters 62–63 ask what “broken” means and why the scripture cannot be broken. This chapter has treated the psalm as standing writing. Standing as cited law is not the finished why.

Chapter 64 asks how God’s Word is truth. This chapter has not examined John 17:17.

Chapter 65 asks why the Graphē is the primary written authority. This chapter has shown that this psalm stands as Holy Writ in force for His hearers in this dispute. Force in this dispute is not the finished gate.

Collapse would make Movement VIII a single file with six titles. The locked TOC forbids that. Sequence is the remedy for collapse, not a slight upon the psalm.

Thus:

> **This chapter is not already Chapters 61–65. Exposition of the citation is not the dedicated reasoning, not unbreakability, not John 17:17, and not the Graphē-gate.**

---

# 60.39 Competing Claim: Psalm Context as Blank Check for Later “Gods” Speculation

The fourth live reduction is the blank check.

The reduction says: because the writing says “Ye are gods,” every later use of that sentence is authorized — deification-systems, identity-teachings detached from judgment, seminars that make the word the whole religion.

The reduction fails because the psalm that contains the sentence also contains unjust judgment, the poor, darkness, death like men, and an appeal to God to judge the earth. A check is not blank if the writing that issues it also writes the limits. The limits are not later piety. They are verses 2–5, 7–8.

The reduction also fails because Christ uses the wording as a written case concerning those to whom the word of God came, in answer to a charge that He, being a man, makes Himself God. He does not use it as a license for the hearers to make themselves the Most High. The application in verse 36, reserved as dedicated reasoning, is already visible as an application to the sanctified and sent Son, not as a distribution of deity to the crowd.

Image and sonship correspondence, already limited in §60.33, do not reopen the check. A real clause plus a real making of man in the image do not equal an unbounded later system. The investigation’s rule remains: what does the writing actually warrant?

Thus:

> **Psalm 82’s context is not a blank check for later “gods” speculation. The same psalm that says “Ye are gods” charges unjust judgment, declares death like men, and appeals to God to judge the earth.**

# 60.40 Reason Through the Evidence

The inference can now be exhibited.

**Premise 1.** John 10:34–36 is Christ’s appeal to what is written as decisive in a blasphemy-dispute; the cited wording is “I said, Ye are gods”; those so called are those to whom the word of God came (Chapter 59).

**Premise 2.** That wording is Psalm 82:6, which stands inside Psalm 82 as a whole.

**Premise 3.** Psalm 82, as a whole, is a judicial argument: God judges those called gods; they judge unjustly; they are commanded to defend the poor; they walk in darkness; they are addressed as gods and children of the Most High; they shall die like men; God is appealed to as judge of the earth.

**Premise 4.** The addressees of that argument, identified by the psalm’s own verbs and by Christ’s characterization, are those who judge under God — those to whom the word of God came — not the Most High, and not an unbounded later “everyone.”

**Premise 5.** A writing-argument requires the words as written. The charge has named God. The psalm already uses that vocabulary as address to commissioned hearers. A paraphrase that avoided, inflated, or thematized the wording would weaken or relocate the exhibit.

**Premise 6.** The psalm is cited as written in their law. It stands as Holy Writ already in force for His hearers (Chapters 48, 52, 58, 59 used, not retried).

**Inference.** Therefore the actual citation, in Psalm 82’s context, is the psalm’s judicial address, directed to those who judge under God and received His word; and He uses the written wording because the case is Scripture-governed argument from that standing exhibit, not from a paraphrase, not from mere opinion, and not from a later slogan about gods.

The inference is not a deduction from a later creed. It is the psalm plus the citation plus the already-established standing of the writing. Alternative global explanations — the psalm as a deification-hymn; the citation as optional colour; this file as already Chapters 61–65; the context as a blank check — fail as accounts of the conjunction, as already shown.

Thus:

> **The warranted inference is that Psalm 82:6, in Psalm 82’s judicial argument, is the standing written address Christ cites, used as wording because the case requires the words as Holy Writ already in force.**

---

# 60.41 Explicit Versus Inferred

Honesty about the inference requires a clean line.

**Explicit.** The sentences of Psalm 82. The wording of John 10:34. The characterization of John 10:35. The identification of the citation as Psalm 82:6. The judicial verbs. The mortality of verse 7. The appeal of verse 8.

**Inferred, as warranted.** That the addressees function as judges under God. That “the word of God came” maps onto the psalm’s “I have said” to that assembly. That He uses the written wording rather than a paraphrase because the case requires the words as exhibit. That the citation is Scripture-governed argument. That later blank-check uses exceed the psalm.

**Not inferred here.** The dedicated a fortiori of John 10:36 as finished logic. The definition of “broken.” The why of unbreakability. John 17:17 as Graphē-doctrine. The Graphē-gate. A completed anthropology of the image. A completed metaphysics of a heavenly council as the chapter’s achievement. Unverifiable details of Asaph, of a particular court-session, or of a scroll in the porch.

The line is the difference between a citation-file and a later-file. Crossing it would be theft. Refusing to infer what the conjunction warrants would be under-claim. The chapter has inferred what the conjunction warrants. It has not inferred what later premises must still supply.

Thus:

> **What is explicit has been distinguished from what is inferred. Later doctrines have not been inferred here. The warranted inferences about addressees, mapping, and written wording have been drawn.**

# 60.42 The Warranted Conclusion Stated with Full Force

The conclusion may now be stated without a remaining apology.

> **Psalm 82 is a judicial psalm. God stands in the congregation and judges those called gods. He charges them with unjust judgment, commands defense of the poor and fatherless, diagnoses their darkness, recalls His prior address — “I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High” — declares that they shall die like men, and appeals to God to judge the earth. That address is directed, in the psalm’s own frame, to those who judge under God, the same persons Christ names as those to whom the word of God came. He cites the written wording, not a paraphrase, because the blasphemy-dispute has named God, and the writing already stands with that vocabulary as Holy Writ in force for His hearers. The investigator is warranted, with full force, in treating this citation as Scripture-governed argument. The psalm’s wording is the exhibit of the court opened in John 10:34–36. This is not yet Christ’s dedicated reasoning from that exhibit. It is not yet “cannot be broken.” It is not yet John 17:17. It is not yet the Graphē-gate. It is not a blank check for later “gods” speculation. It is the actual citation in its Psalm 82 context, and the reason He uses the written wording. That is this chapter’s conclusion.**

The remaining questions follow by sequence. The citation is already in force.

The scope of this stage is the actual citation and its Psalm 82 context, with the reason the written wording is used.

It includes the psalm as a whole, the addressees as those who judge under God and received His word, the correspondence of verse 6 to John 10:34–35, and the reason a paraphrase would weaken the case.

The scope is not a delay. It is the assignment. An assignment performed with full force is not a partial assignment. It is this assignment, complete.

Thus:

Thus:

# 60.45 From the Citation to Christ’s Reasoning From What Is Written

An actual citation, now examined in the psalm’s own argument as standing written wording, still leaves a further question.

The citation-file is in force. He has cited “I said, Ye are gods.” The wording has been located in Psalm 82’s judicial address to those who judge under God, those to whom the word of God came. The reason He uses the written wording rather than a paraphrase has been stated. Those sentences are the cleared ground. They are not yet the dedicated examination of how He reasons from that wording to the present charge, nor of the weight He assigns to the written text in that reasoning.

If the wording were not examined in the psalm, the next question would still be what the writing is. The writing has been examined. If this chapter were already that later reasoning, the next file would be repetition. This chapter is not that later reasoning. The next question is therefore the construction the locked assignment names: Christ’s reasoning from what is written — the logic of the argument and the weight He assigns to the written text.

That is the proper open of the next chapter. Psalm 82:6 was never meant to be a slogan about gods, and it was never meant to finish Movement VIII at the second step. It was meant to be the actual citation in context, sufficient to justify taking the next question, which is the question a cited writing itself forces once it has been heard as writing: how does He reason from it?

# Chapter Summary

> **The chapter’s central conclusion:** Psalm 82, read as a complete argument, is a judicial psalm in which God judges those He has addressed as gods — those who judge under Him, who fail the poor, who shall die like men, those to whom the word of God came. Verse 6, “I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High,” is that prior address in its place. Christ cites the written wording, not a paraphrase, because the blasphemy-dispute has named God and the writing already stands with that vocabulary as Holy Writ in force for His hearers. Competing reductions fail: “gods” as the whole point without the judicial frame; ignoring the appeal to written law; this chapter as already Chapters 61–65; the psalm as a blank check for later speculation. The investigator is warranted, with full force, in receiving this citation as Scripture-governed argument. The dedicated reasoning from the wording remains later because it is a later question. Movement VIII continues. The second verdict of Movement VIII is in force.

The essential architecture is:

> **Opening of the passage already stated → actual citation defined → Psalm 82 context defined → why written wording defined → lexical control → psalm given in full → argument followed verse by verse → addressees identified from the psalm and from Christ’s characterization → correspondence of citation → paraphrase refused as a weakened exhibit → standing as Holy Writ for His hearers → positive warrant → failure of reductions → citation-file warranted → sequence to Christ’s reasoning from what is written.**

The governing distinctions are:

- **Actual citation** is not **theme, expansion, or invented setting**.
- **Psalm 82 context** is not **a detached lemma**.
- **Why He uses the written wording** is not **Chapter 61**.
- **Exposition of the psalm** is not **Chapters 62–63**.
- **Judicial frame** is not **optional colour**.
- **Sonship / image correspondence** is not **a blank check**.
- **This file** is not **Chapter 59 retried**, not **a modern quarrel as center**, and not **the Graphē-gate**.
- **Scripture-governed argument** is not **mere opinion** and not **a new oracle**.
- **Limits** are **the shape of the doctrine**, not **delayed doubt**.
- **Sequence** is **not hesitation about this level**.

The decisive principle is:

> **Examine the actual citation of Psalm 82:6 in its Psalm 82 context, claiming what that psalm and that citation warrant and not more: the wording is the psalm’s judicial address to those who judge under God and received His word, used as written because the case requires the words as Holy Writ already in force, before the dedicated reasoning-file, before the finished why of unbreakability, before John 17:17, and before the Graphē-gate. Draw the conclusion the premises support. Do not draw the conclusions that still require later premises. Then ask how He reasons from what is written.**
